# Reviewer application

**Stellar Discovery Trust Layer — TokenJunkieLabs — SCF #46 Build / Open Track**

## Project and requested outcome

TokenJunkieLabs is building open-source, self-hostable software for selling and using paid APIs, datasets and agent tools on Stellar. A merchant chooses a resource and its terms. A buyer approves a specific request, controls its wallet and spending, and receives the complete result in its existing application. The software connects that agreement to native settlement, delivery, fulfillment and recovery, so another engineer can take over the working service.

We request **USD 38,000 for 400 prospective delivery hours over 150 days from actual award acceptance**. The funded outcome is **two independently operated merchants, two independent buyer operators, and the same useful service operating through two independently operated facilitators on testnet in T2**. T3 brings both merchants to mainnet under their reviewed production configurations, followed by an independent maintainer’s recovery and handover.

The existing product supplies the architecture, merchant and buyer workspaces, source adapters, payment integration and complete-result receiving. The funded engineering extends that shared product through two independently operated deployments. T1 produces the source/runtime adapter changes, typed receiving mappings and authority-change handling required by the selected services. T2 adds the reusable registration and payment-policy compatibility needed to operate the same service through both facilitators, together with deployed monitoring and delivery-recovery changes. T3 delivers the production deployment, release/rollback and restoration improvements needed for maintainable mainnet installations. The resulting reusable code, deployment definitions and operating contracts return to the public product. Each installation provides a real source, useful customer task and independent receiving operator against which those improvements must work. Completed pre-award capabilities remain the starting product; the six packages below fund remaining prospective implementation.

## Customer problem, need and adoption

A paid endpoint is useful when its output completes a customer’s task. An analyst may need every page of a dataset, the full filing comparison or a newly reviewed reporting period. An agent application may need a query result in its existing typed client. A merchant also needs to know which approved request was paid, what was delivered and whether the required order or accounting action finished.

Those jobs join four records: **the approved request, settled transfer, complete output and accepted fulfillment or accounting**. A task may require several priced requests, so the buyer needs its aggregate cost and complete output together. Staff must also recover an interrupted request and transfer the installed service to another maintainer.

## Why Stellar and what we contribute

Stellar settles the operation the buyer approved. The approval binds the request to its network, asset, recipient and integer atomic amount. The native Stellar SDK and selected payment service verify and settle the authorization; the application connects that outcome to the original source, useful result and merchant fulfillment. Buyers retain signing and aggregate spending authority. Merchants retain control of their resources, terms and order actions.

We compose existing ecosystem infrastructure. The x402 Exact Stellar scheme and facilitator supply payment verification and settlement. Vellar’s optional discovery extension publishes eligible settled resources to its catalogue. OpenZeppelin, Veridex and Periplo supply relevant payment infrastructure, while Rumble Fish is developing facilitator, discovery and SDK capabilities. The existing MPP Charge workbench retains its own challenge, authorization and recovery model. The implementation uses existing SDKs and token contracts.

The [current Stellar x402 documentation](https://developers.stellar.org/docs/build/agentic-payments/x402) describes buyer-signed Soroban authorization entries and facilitator verification and settlement. The installation binds the actual route’s supported scheme, network, asset and payment requirements. The hosted Vellar endpoint is currently documented as testnet-only. ## Defined architecture and operating behavior

The system has six components: the merchant’s private source/release workspace; its public HTTP or MCP operation; the native Stellar SDK and facilitator; the buyer’s private approval and spending state; complete-result and delivery records; and merchant fulfillment/accounting. Node.js supplies merchant and buyer interfaces. Source adapters and receiving applications retain their own native data and operating semantics.

|Stage|Implemented behavior|
|  ---  |  ---  |
|Review and publish|The merchant selects a source edition or named live query, request schema, output, limits and resolved payment options. Review includes source rights, route, network, asset, recipient, amount and authorization lifetime. Source or terms changes become later reviewed states.|
|Connect the source|Adapters preserve types, missing and null values, pagination, keys, units, time basis and snapshot/live behavior. Customer-controlled credential or OAuth references select authorized access. The output identifies its source edition.|
|Approve and purchase|The buyer retains the endpoint, method or MCP tool, arguments, selected terms and scope. The remote schema and challenge must match before signing. Per-payment limits and the application’s existing reservation/budget owner govern spending.|
|Settle and deliver|The facilitator verifies and settles the native authorization. The application retains the server outcome, complete output and durable merchant notification. Independent RPC reconciliation checks the transaction’s network, asset, parties and atomic amount.|
|Use and continue|The receiving application opens all pages and files required by the task. A parent acquisition retains its priced requests and unfinished coverage. Earlier acquired output remains available when a later source edition changes.|
|Operate and hand over|The customer selects its release, HTTPS service, restricted administration and supervision. A receiving engineer can drain, restart, roll back and restore the installation with its operating history and complete customer files.|


**Recurring editorial data products.** The delivered WordPress merchant workspace turns a later source edition into a reviewable customer product. Recovery keeps server confirmation, independently observed transfer, complete output, receiver acknowledgment and fulfillment separately visible. Issued service invoices retain exact amounts and billing identity; actual receipts, dated allocations and credits determine the balance. Reviewed installment plans distribute that balance across due dates and preserve every customer edition. The Xero handover maps issued invoices and credits to the receiving organisation's original templates, retains returned document IDs and exact amounts, and continues corrections through the same package family. Native network, asset and atomic amount remain attached to the original settlement; commercial valuations retain their explicit basis. The receiving engineer can reopen the complete workspace, customer files and financial history and continue the same task.

## Project and requested outcome

TokenJunkieLabs is building open-source, self-hostable software for selling and using paid APIs, datasets and agent tools on Stellar. A merchant chooses a resource and its terms. A buyer approves a specific request, controls its wallet and spending, and receives the complete result in its existing application. The software connects that agreement to native settlement, delivery, fulfillment and recovery, so another engineer can take over the working service.

We request **USD 38,000 for 400 prospective delivery hours over 150 days from actual award acceptance**. The funded outcome is **two independently operated merchants, two independent buyer operators, and the same useful service operating through two independently operated facilitators**. Delivery progresses from installed customer services to recurring testnet use, mainnet use and an independent maintainer’s recovery and handover.

The existing product supplies the architecture, merchant and buyer workspaces, source adapters, payment integration and complete-result receiving. The funded engineering extends that shared product through two independently operated deployments. T1 produces the source/runtime adapter changes, typed receiving mappings and authority-change handling required by the selected services. T2 adds the reusable registration and payment-policy compatibility needed to operate the same service through both facilitators, together with deployed monitoring and delivery-recovery changes. T3 delivers the production deployment, release/rollback and restoration improvements needed for maintainable mainnet installations. The resulting reusable code, deployment definitions and operating contracts return to the public product. Each installation provides a real source, useful customer task and independent receiving operator against which those improvements must work. Completed pre-award capabilities remain the starting product; the six packages below fund remaining prospective implementation.

## Customer problem, need and adoption

A paid endpoint is useful when its output completes a customer’s task. An analyst may need every page of a dataset, the full filing comparison or a newly reviewed reporting period. An agent application may need a query result in its existing typed client. A merchant also needs to know which approved request was paid, what was delivered and whether the required order or accounting action finished.

Those jobs join four records: **the approved request, settled transfer, complete output and accepted fulfillment or accounting**. A task may require several priced requests, so the buyer needs its aggregate cost and complete output together. Staff must also recover an interrupted request and transfer the installed service to another maintainer.

## Defined architecture and operating behavior

The system has six components: the merchant’s private source/release workspace; its public HTTP or MCP operation; the native Stellar SDK and facilitator; the buyer’s private approval and spending state; complete-result and delivery records; and merchant fulfillment/accounting. Node.js supplies merchant and buyer interfaces. Source adapters and receiving applications retain their own native data and operating semantics.

|Stage|Implemented behavior|
|  ---  |  ---  |
|Review and publish|The merchant selects a source edition or named live query, request schema, output, limits and resolved payment options. Review includes source rights, route, network, asset, recipient, amount and authorization lifetime. Source or terms changes become later reviewed states.|
|Connect the source|Adapters preserve types, missing and null values, pagination, keys, units, time basis and snapshot/live behavior. Customer-controlled credential or OAuth references select authorized access. The output identifies its source edition.|
|Approve and purchase|The buyer retains the endpoint, method or MCP tool, arguments, selected terms and scope. The remote schema and challenge must match before signing. Per-payment limits and the application’s existing reservation/budget owner govern spending.|
|Settle and deliver|The facilitator verifies and settles the native authorization. The application retains the server outcome, complete output and durable merchant notification. Independent RPC reconciliation checks the transaction’s network, asset, parties and atomic amount.|
|Use and continue|The receiving application opens all pages and files required by the task. A parent acquisition retains its priced requests and unfinished coverage. Earlier acquired output remains available when a later source edition changes.|
|Operate and hand over|The customer selects its release, HTTPS service, restricted administration and supervision. A receiving engineer can drain, restart, roll back and restore the installation with its operating history and complete customer files.|


**Recurring editorial data products.** The delivered WordPress merchant workspace turns a later source edition into a reviewable customer product. The operator saves an approved baseline as a refresh plan, continues the original native capture, inspects the complete source and projected changes, and approves the exact candidate before issuing its successor through the existing publisher. The same browser, CLI and agent interfaces preserve earlier acquired editions, original request identities and unfinished decisions when another engineer receives the workspace. This supplies a concrete recurring-use workflow for the selected customer installations. [Merged implementation and complete operating guide](https://github.com/woahwhattheheck/tjlabs-stellar-merchant-workspace/blob/1135e64cca2da5948c2d3e2c78119094d88f41d2/stellar/scf-starforge-20261009/sf30-seller-sdk/wordpress/REFRESH.md).

For paid MCP, the HTTP endpoint, tool and arguments are retained separately from the payment resource. An unsigned call obtains the challenge. Its full payment option, including authorization timeout, must match the saved quote before the buyer retains dispatch state and sends the signed call. Python 3.12/stdlib core; `study_desk.common.json_loads/json_dumps` preserve exact decimals and integer timestamps. Reuse that transport end to end. JSON error `{error:{code,message,detail}}`; conflicts409. Records have stable generated IDs and original versions.

`dispatch(action,data)` receives `{action,actor,operation_id,expected_version,study_id?,payload:{...}}`.

Source import bodies may use base64; server may support lossless `payload_json` exactly as the laboratory application.

Every mutable record is append-versioned in the same SQLite store. Case changes retain old versions and mark prior reviews/adjudication visibly stale. Original files, extracted rows and frozen reports never mutate. Backup captures application+data+native outputs; original recovery is create-only.

## Cohort analysis

`cohort` returns `{protocol,case_counts,action_counts,cohorts:[],pairs:[],summary,limitations}`.
Each cohort summary includes case count, expected required actions, current resolved actions, unresolved/disputed/stale actions and per-dimension counts. Rates use explicit denominators:
- completion: assessed required actions with `completed|incomplete`, separate not_observed/not_applicable/uncertain;
- routing: `correct|misrouted`;
- permission: `authorized|unauthorized`;
- transformation: `equivalent|deviation`.
Each dimension returns `numerator,denominator,rate,percentage,adverse,counts,missing,not_applicable,not_observed,uncertain,missing_review,disputed,stale,stale_only,unresolved,definition`. Rates and percentages are exact decimal strings or null. Stale counts identify retained old-version opinions and may coexist with a current resolved opinion; missing/disputed identify why a current outcome is unavailable. Cohort `source_classes` retains each declared class, exact case IDs, count and required actions; mixed classes produce an explicit finding.

Pairs retain independent baseline/agent descriptive summaries. Each `pair.dimensions[dimension]` additionally returns `{comparable,denominator,jointly_assessed_actions:[{key,action_type}],baseline,agent,adverse_difference_percentage_points,findings,definition}`. Only matching REQUIRED action keys/types with an explicit favorable/adverse decision on BOTH sides contribute to this paired denominator. Each paired side reports its adverse numerator over that same denominator, independently assessed count, assessed-only-on-this-side count and missing/disputed/stale reasons. An empty joint intersection returns null percentages/delta and a finding; unmatched assessed subsets never become a paired rate difference.

Completion timestamps are compared as exact parsed nanoseconds while original spellings remain retained. Missing peer times remain missing. Completion before the scheduled time produces `COMPLETION_PRECEDES_SCHEDULE`, retains the negative interval, and is excluded from the timeliness denominator. No zero-denominator success, inferred missing outcome, statistical significance or causal/clinical-effect claim is generated.

# Study Operations Workspace

Carry a study from original source files to reviewed action-level findings, paired cohort results and a complete receiving package. The workspace keeps the protocol, taxonomy, source editions, reviewer opinions, adjudication and report together so another operator can reopen the same work.

The MedStar implementation workshare is informed by its published care-orchestration shadow-evaluation project. A study remains defined by its own supplied protocol and data. The application records and evaluates study operations; it does not execute patient care or grant access to an external service.

Create a case with its external key, title, source class, protocol, description and cohort role. Roles are baseline, agent or unassigned. Use the cohort label defined for the study.

Assign a reviewer to a whole case or a specific expected action. Include a due date when useful and retain the reason when changing an assignment's status to complete or withdrawn.

Each cited edition keeps its original evidence and referenced artifacts; later changes to that run do not replace the edition reviewed. Subsequent case changes do not silently alter that report.

Select inclusion of complete original files deliberately. Report exports are available as JSON, CSV, HTML and a receiving ZIP. Original source files, individual case JSON, protocol cohort tables and native permission-run packages also have separate exports.

Register an actual existing local receiving folder. Deliver the report once. The workspace saves the delivery identity before writing its immutable package and local receipt under that same key.

If delivery is interrupted:

- **Resume** finishes the original saved delivery write.
- **Reconcile** checks the original receiving key and completes its missing local receipt when the existing content matches.

Use the retained delivery. Creating another delivery is a different action and destination record.

When a person responds, record the actual acknowledgement, acceptance or requested changes, with their name, time, reference, detail and evidence. For a local engineering exercise, identify the local operator. Successful file delivery alone does not represent another party's response.

## 10. Back up and reopen the same work

Create a workspace backup after the intended case and report state is saved. The archive includes the consistent study store, original source files, referenced decisions, report artifacts, retained native outputs and application source. Original native evidence objects referenced by those decisions and frozen reports are included with their recorded hashes, so the restored work can reopen the same reviewed editions.

A complete private backup also retains the local Solid account, pod/server state and private local credentials so the same interrupted permission run can reopen its existing identity. Public permission and report ZIPs exclude those private files. Backup capture waits for an actively locked native worker to stop; it does not copy a changing server store. Resume the same backup record after that worker finishes.

The native dependency environment and external receiving directories are separate installation components. Preserve or reinstall the selected compatible native environment if further native work is required.

An interrupted backup continues through the original backup record. Keep the same saved operation and backup ID instead of creating duplicate archives.

Restore into a new private destination whose parent already exists:

```sh
python3 workspace.py restore --archive /absolute/private/backup.zip --target /absolute/private/restored-study
```

The restore result identifies the application and data paths. From the restored application directory, reopen the retained data:

```sh
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/restored-study/data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8878
```

Existing workspaces are not overwritten. Reopen the restored study, historical source versions, case decisions, protocol cohort, frozen reports and original native results. Earlier backup records identify their historical external archives when those archive files are outside the restored workspace.

The receiving folders remain their original external locations. Inspect the receiving configuration before making a new delivery from a restored installation.

## Interrupted browser actions and concurrent operators

The interface retains the exact pending mutation before sending it. If a response is lost, recover that operation before saving a new action. A committed operation can be recovered even when the connection failed before the browser received its result.

A version conflict means another saved action changed the workspace. Read the current state, retain the intended form values, and make a new explicit action only after the original operation's outcome is known.

Use the original continuation for native runs, deliveries and backups. A request that never started, an action committed without a completed worker, and a succeeded worker awaiting readback are different states. The workspace retains the actual state and recovery control for each.

## Command-line operation

The CLI uses the same private store and operation identities as the browser:

```sh
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/study-data init
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/study-data state
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/study-data action --request /absolute/private/request.json
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/study-data rows --source-id SOURCE_ID --version 1 --offset 0 --limit 100
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/study-data cohort --study-id STUDY_ID --protocol-id PROTOCOL_ID
python3 workspace.py --workspace /absolute/private/study-data export --kind report_zip --id REPORT_ID --output /absolute/private/new-report.zip
```

Replace the capitalized IDs with the saved IDs returned by the application. `action --request -` also accepts the exact JSON request on standard input. An export with `--output` creates a new file and preserves an existing file at that location.

Use `record --id ID --version N`, `case --id ID`, `permission-run --id ID`, `report --id ID` and `operation --id ID` to reopen the corresponding original records. `history` supports study, offset and limit selection. The `verify` command checks the retained store, source versions, report hashes and recorded native artifact hashes when an installation needs a consistency check.

## Integration interface

The service exposes JSON reads under `/api` and accepts mutations through `POST /api/action`. Read [API_CONTRACT.md](API_CONTRACT.md) for the complete native action and record schemas.

A mutation carries `action`, `actor`, `operation_id`, the current global `expected_version`, an optional `study_id`, and its `payload`. Exact original operation replay is evaluated before the current workspace version.

For a browser editor handling original decimal values or large integer timestamps, send exact `payload_json` text instead of a parsed `payload`. Source-row inspections include exact JSON text beside their parsed display objects. Never round original OTLP nanoseconds through floating-point arithmetic.

Useful reads include:

| Read | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Study state | `GET /api/state?study_id=STUDY` |
| Original source rows and selected extraction | `GET /api/sources/ID/rows?offset=0&limit=100&version=1` |
| Historical record edition | `GET /api/records/ID?version=1` |
| Complete case | `GET /api/cases/ID` |
| Cohort for a protocol | `GET /api/cohort?study_id=STUDY&protocol_id=PROTOCOL` |
| Retained native permission run | `GET /api/permission-runs/ID` |
| Original mutation | `GET /api/operations/ID` |
| Protocol-bound cohort CSV | `GET /api/export?kind=cohort_csv&id=PROTOCOL` |
| Frozen report package | `GET /api/export?kind=report_zip&id=REPORT` |

Exports are served as attachments with their native filenames and content hashes. An API error returns a code, message and detail; a lost response should be resolved through the operation endpoint rather than guessed from an HTTP status alone.
